options.B: The “scarlet letter” of the title refers to the letter ‘A’.
options.D: It was written in the 19th century.

infoBite: Hawthorne's The Scarlet Letter (1850): Hester Prynne wears an “A” for adultery in Puritan Boston. It opens with “The Custom-House” sketch and is not told in letters. Also asked in GATE 2026.

question:
“[…] I mean negative capability, that is when a man is capable of being in uncertainties, mysteries, doubts, without any irritable reaching after fact and reason […].”
Based on this statement, which of the following options is/are correct?
Negative capability is the ability to _______ .

options.C: not get irritated by people’s incompetence

works: Letter to George and Tom Keats (December 1817)
infoBite: From Keats's letter to his brothers George and Tom (December 1817), naming Shakespeare as the poet who had this quality “so enormously”. Keats contrasts it with Coleridge's restless reaching after knowledge.

question:
Virginia Woolf wrote in “Professions for Women”:
“You have won rooms of your own in the house hitherto exclusively owned by men. You are able, though not without great labour and effort, to pay the rent. You are earning your five hundred pounds a year. But this freedom is only a beginning; the room is your own, but it is still bare. It has to be furnished; it has to be decorated; it has to be shared. How are you going to furnish it, how are you going to decorate it? With whom are you going to share it, and upon what terms?”
Based on this passage, which of the following inferences is/are correct?

options.A: Women may have attained rooms of their own but they still have a long way to go.
options.B: The ‘room’ women now own is a sign of minimal economic independence.
options.C: Woolf insists that women live only with other women in order to maintain their independence.
options.D: The freedom that women now enjoy was attained after centuries of struggle.

infoBite: “Professions for Women” was a 1931 talk to the National Society for Women's Service, where Woolf describes killing the “Angel in the House” (Coventry Patmore's phrase). The room and £500 echo A Room of One's Own (1929).

question: Which of the following statements is/are correct?

options.A: Rasa is a form of categorizing a text by its genre.
options.B: According to Abhinavagupta, Rasa is best experienced collectively and in unison with others.
options.C: Rasa is purely an aesthetic emotion, not to be confused with real-life emotions.
options.D: Rasa is evoked only by performances like drama and dance.

infoBite: Abhinavagupta's Abhinavabhāratī, a commentary on Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra, treats rasa as a generalised, impersonal relish (sādhāraṇīkaraṇa) enjoyed by the sahṛdaya, not a private real-life emotion. Rasa theory also came up in GATE 2025.

question:
“Lear cries out ‘you are men of stones’
as Cordelia hangs from a broken wall.
I step out into Chandni Chowk, a street once
strewn with jasmine flowers
for the Empress and the royal women
who bought perfumes from Isfahan,
fabrics from Dacca, essence from Kabul,
glass bangles from Agra.
Beggars now live here in tombs
of unknown nobles and forgotten saints
while hawkers sell combs and mirrors
outside a Sikh temple. Across the street,
a theater is showing a Bombay spectacular.
I think of Zafar, poet and Emperor,
being led through this street
by British soldiers, his feet in chains,
to watch his sons hanged.
In exile he wrote:
‘Unfortunate Zafar
spent half his life in hope,
the other half waiting.
He begs for two yards of Delhi for burial.’
He was exiled to Burma, buried in Rangoon.”
Which of the following ideas is/are conveyed by this poem?

options.A: Delhi is a modern and progressive city despite its imperial past.
options.B: Even Kings may be punished when they commit crimes against their children.
options.C: An exile’s sense of loss, and longing for their homeland.
options.D: History is a constant presence all around us.

infoBite: Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor, was exiled to Rangoon after 1857 and died there in 1862; the lines echo his ghazal lament for “do gaz zameen” (two yards of earth). Lear's “men of stones” is from King Lear, Act 5, Scene 3.
note: The paper does not name the poem or poet, and the attribution couldn't be confirmed, so the poet is left untagged.

question:
Which of the following statements is/are true of these novels:
Anna Karenina, Dead Souls, Crime and Punishment, Fathers and Sons.

options.A: They are all written by Russian authors.
options.B: They all have women as central protagonists.
options.C: They were all written in the 19th century.
options.D: They all highlight socially transgressive romantic relationships.

infoBite: Dead Souls (Gogol, 1842), Fathers and Sons (Turgenev, 1862), Crime and Punishment (Dostoevsky, 1866), Anna Karenina (Tolstoy, 1877). Only Anna Karenina has a woman at its centre.

question:
“[…] in so far as the academic discourse of history – that is, ‘history’ as a discourse produced at the institutional site of the university – is concerned, ‘Europe’ remains the sovereign, theoretical subject of all histories, including the ones we call ‘Indian,’ ‘Chinese,’ ‘Kenyan,’ and so on. There is a peculiar way in which all these other histories tend to become variations on a master narrative that could be called ‘the history of Europe.’ In this sense, ‘Indian’ history itself is in a position of subalternity; one can only articulate subaltern subject positions in the name of this history.”
Which of the following options is/are implied by the passage above?

options.A: People in postcolonial societies are condemned to endlessly repeat their own histories.
options.B: The histories of India, China, and Kenya are not fundamentally different from one another.
options.C: Within the protocols of history writing, it is impossible to write the history of postcolonial societies without reference to Europe.
options.D: Instead of Europe, India should be the sovereign subject of all histories.

works: Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History
infoBite: From Dipesh Chakrabarty's “Postcoloniality and the Artifice of History” (1992), expanded in Provincializing Europe (2000). Chakrabarty belongs to the Subaltern Studies collective begun by Ranajit Guha.

question:
“What if, in order to save some humans lost in their language, in order to deliver the humans themselves, at the expense of their language, it was better to renounce the language, at least to renounce the best conditions for survival ‘at all costs’ for the idiom? And what if some humans were more worth saving than their language, under circumstances where, alas, one needed to choose between them? For we are living in a period in which the question at times arises. Today, on this earth of humans, certain people must yield to the homo-hegemony of dominant languages. They must learn the language of the masters, of capital and machines; they must lose their idiom in order to survive or live better.”
On the basis of this passage, which of the following options is/are correct?
The writer of this passage is:

options.A: Advocating that all colonized people should renounce their native languages to succeed in a globalized world.
options.B: Lamenting that in our contemporary world, some groups of people are forced to choose between immersion in their own language and economic survival.
options.C: Implicitly expressing despair about the hegemony of dominant languages.
options.D: Suggesting that there should be only one language in the world.

infoBite: The writer laments, rather than advocates, the pressure to give up one's idiom for the “language of the masters”. Compare Ngũgĩ's case for writing in Gikuyu (Q32 of this paper).
note: The paper does not name the source and the author couldn't be confirmed, so no writer is tagged.

question:
Politics — by William Butler Yeats
‘In our time the destiny of man presents its meanings in political terms.’ — Thomas Mann
“How can I, that girl standing there,
My attention fix
On Roman or on Russian
Or on Spanish politics,
Yet here’s a travelled man that knows
What he talks about,
And there’s a politician
That has both read and thought,
And maybe what they say is true
Of war and war’s alarms,
But O that I were young again
And held her in my arms.”
Which of the following options is/are implied by this poem?

options.A: Politics is the most absorbing concern of human existence.
options.B: Desire has never distracted the speaker from politics.
options.C: Sensual desire can be in conflict with cerebral concerns.
options.D: Physical desire does not die with age.

infoBite: “Politics” (1938) is among Yeats's last poems and closes Last Poems (1939). Its epigraph from Thomas Mann is answered with desire over public affairs. Yeats was also asked in GATE 2025.

question:
“Although feminist philosophers have traditionally sought to show how the body is figured as feminine, or how women have been associated with materiality (whether inert – always already dead – or fecund – ever-living and procreative) where men have been associated with the principle of rational mastery, Irigaray wants to argue that in fact the feminine is precisely what is excluded in and by such a binary opposition. In this sense, when and where women are represented within this economy is precisely the site of their erasure.”
Which of the following options is/are implied by this passage?

options.A: Irigaray’s work does not replicate the stance of traditional feminist philosophy.
options.B: Irigaray radically questions the mind/body distinction from a feminist perspective.
options.C: For Irigaray, the place assigned to women, even by some feminist philosophers, may in fact serve to erase them.
options.D: Irigaray is not crucially concerned about the feminine.

works: This Sex Which Is Not One
infoBite: Luce Irigaray, with Hélène Cixous and Julia Kristeva, is a key French feminist; her major works are Speculum of the Other Woman (1974) and This Sex Which Is Not One (1977).

question:
“I like a look of Agony,
Because I know it’s true –
Men do not sham Convulsion,
Nor simulate, a Throe –
The eyes glaze once – and that is Death –
Impossible to feign
The Beads upon the Forehead
By homely Anguish strung.”
Which of the following options is/are implied by this poem?

options.B: The speaker likes to watch people suffer because it reminds her of her own wellbeing.
options.C: Strong people never suffer a painful death.

works: I like a look of Agony
infoBite: Emily Dickinson's poem (c. 1861) values agony because it cannot be faked. Note her dashes, capitalised nouns and slant rhyme; most of her poems were published only after her death in 1886.

question:
“We dwell with satisfaction upon the poet’s difference from his predecessors, especially his immediate predecessors; […]. Whereas if we approach a poet without this prejudice we shall often find that not only the best, but the most individual parts of his works may be those in which the dead poets, his ancestors, assert their immortality most vigorously.”
Which of the following options is/are implied by this excerpt?

options.A: Being different from one’s predecessors need not be the defining characteristic of a good poet.
options.B: What we consider original in a poem, may be deeply rooted in tradition.
options.C: There is no difference between old and new poems.
options.D: The past is often a living presence in good contemporary poetry.

infoBite: From T. S. Eliot's “Tradition and the Individual Talent” (1919), on the “historical sense”. The same essay supplied GATE 2026's “escape from personality” passage, so read it whole.

question: Which factor(s) led to the rise and popularity of the novel in England?

options.B: The spread of printing presses throughout England.
options.C: The migration of large numbers of writers and intellectuals from Italy.

infoBite: Ian Watt's The Rise of the Novel (1957) links the form to a growing literate middle-class readership, print culture and circulating libraries, with Defoe, Richardson and Fielding as the founders.

question:
Rafi told Mary, “I am thinking of watching a film this weekend.”
The following reports the above statement in indirect speech:
Rafi told Mary that he _______ of watching a film that weekend.
infoBite: After a past reporting verb (“told”), present continuous shifts back to past continuous: “am thinking” → “was thinking”, and “this weekend” → “that weekend”.

question:
Permit : _______ : : Enforce : Relax
(By word meaning)
infoBite: “Enforce” and “relax” are opposites, so “permit” pairs with its opposite, “forbid”.

question: Given a fair six-faced dice where the faces are labelled ‘1’, ‘2’, ‘3’, ‘4’, ‘5’, and ‘6’, what is the probability of getting a ‘1’ on the first roll of the dice and a ‘4’ on the second roll?
infoBite: The two rolls are independent, so multiply: 1/6 × 1/6 = 1/36.

question:
A recent survey shows that 65% of tobacco users were advised to stop consuming tobacco. The survey also shows that 3 out of 10 tobacco users attempted to stop using tobacco.
Based only on the information in the above passage, which one of the following options can be logically inferred with certainty?

options.A: A majority of tobacco users who were advised to stop consuming tobacco made an attempt to do so.
options.B: A majority of tobacco users who were advised to stop consuming tobacco did not attempt to do so.
options.C: Approximately 30% of tobacco users successfully stopped consuming tobacco.
options.D: Approximately 65% of tobacco users successfully stopped consuming tobacco.

infoBite: 65 in 100 were advised but only 30 in 100 tried, so even if every one who tried had been advised, fewer than half of the advised attempted. Nothing is said about success, so C and D can't be inferred.

question:
Students of all the departments of a college who have successfully completed the registration process are eligible to vote in the upcoming college elections. However, by the time the due date for registration was over, it was found that suprisingly none of the students from the Department of Human Sciences had completed the registration process.
Based only on the information provided above, which one of the following sets of statement(s) can be logically inferred with certainty?
(i) All those students who would not be eligible to vote in the college elections would certainly belong to the Department of Human Sciences.
(ii) None of the students from departments other than Human Sciences failed to complete the registration process within the due time.
(iii) All the eligible voters would certainly be students who are not from the Department of Human Sciences.
infoBite: Only registered students can vote and no Human Sciences student registered, so every eligible voter is from another department (iii). (i) and (ii) assume everyone else registered, which isn't stated.

question:
Which one of the options does NOT describe the passage below or follow from it?
We tend to think of cancer as a ‘modern’ illness because its metaphors are so modern. It is a disease of overproduction, of sudden growth, a growth that is unstoppable, tipped into the abyss of no control. Modern cell biology encourages us to imagine the cell as a molecular machine. Cancer is that machine unable to quench its intial command (to grow) and thus transform into an indestructible, self-propelled automaton.
[Adapted from The Emperor of All Maladies by Siddhartha Mukherjee]

options.A: It is a reflection of why cancer seems so modern to most of us.
options.B: It tells us that modern cell biology uses and promotes metaphors of machinery.
options.C: Modern cell biology encourages metaphors of machinery, and cancer is often imagined as a machine.
options.D: Modern cell biology never uses figurative language, such as metaphors, to describe or explain anything.

infoBite: The passage itself shows cell biology using a machine metaphor, so D contradicts it. Mukherjee's The Emperor of All Maladies (2010) won the 2011 Pulitzer Prize for General Nonfiction.

question: The digit in the unit’s place of the product 3^999 × 7^1000 is _______.
infoBite: Last digits of powers of 3 cycle 3, 9, 7, 1 and of 7 cycle 7, 9, 3, 1. 999 leaves remainder 3 when divided by 4, so 3^999 ends in 7; 7^1000 ends in 1. 7 × 1 = 7.
note: Exponents are typeset in the original; written here with ^.

question: Which word below best describes the idea of being both Spineless and Cowardly?
infoBite: Pusillanimous = timid, lacking courage. Unctuous = oily and flattering; obsequious = too eager to please; reticent = reserved, saying little.

question:
Choose the right preposition to fill up the blank:
The whole family got together ___ Diwali
infoBite: Use “at” for a festival or holiday period (at Diwali, at Christmas) and “on” for the particular day (on Diwali day).

question:
Select the correct option to fill in all the blanks to complete the passage:
The (i)_______ factor amid this turbulence has been the (ii)________ of high-octane, action-oriented films such as RRR, K.G.F: Chapter 2 and Pushpa from film industries in the south of the country. Traditionally, films made in the south have done well in their own (iii) _________. But increasingly, their dubbed versions have performed well in the Hindi heartland, with collections (iv)________ those of their Bollywood counterparts.
infoBite: “Amid this turbulence” plus “performed well” signals a positive turn: the redeeming factor was the southern films' outperformance, with collections eclipsing Bollywood's.

question:
The following passage consists of 6 sentences. The first and sixth sentences of the passage are at their correct positions, while the middle four sentences (represented by 2, 3, 4, and 5) are jumbled up.
Choose the correct sequence of the sentences so that they form a coherent paragraph:
1. Most obviously, mobility is taken to be a geographical as well as a social phenomenon.
2. Much of the social mobility literature regarded society as a uniform surface and failed to register the geographical intersections of region, city and place, with the social categories of class, gender and ethnicity.
3. The existing sociology of migration is incidentally far too limited in its concerns to be very useful here.
4. Further, I am concerned with the flows of people within, but especially beyond, the territory of each society, and how these flows may relate to many different desires, for work, housing, leisure, religion, family relationships, criminal gain, asylum seeking and so on.
5. Moreover, not only people are mobile but so too are many ‘objects’.
6. I show that sociology’s recent development of a ‘sociology of objects’ needs to be taken further and that the diverse flows of objects across societal borders and their intersections with the multiple flows of people are hugely significant.
infoBite: Sentence 2 explains “geographical as well as social”, 3 adds an aside on migration studies, “Further” (4) adds the next concern, and “Moreover… objects” (5) leads into 6 on the sociology of objects.

question: The population of a country increased by 5% from 2020 to 2021. Then, the population decreased by 5% from 2021 to 2022. By what percentage did the population change from 2020 to 2022?
infoBite: 1.05 × 0.95 = 0.9975, a net fall of 0.25%. An equal percentage rise and fall never cancel out.

question: The words Thin: Slim: Slender are related in some way. Identify the correct option(s) that reflect(s) the same relationship:
infoBite: Thin, slim and slender name the same quality in increasingly flattering words; so do fat/plump/voluptuous and short/small/petite. Tall/taller/tallest is degrees of comparison.

question:
A pandemic like situation hit the country last year, resulting in loss of human life and economic depression. To improve the condition of its citizens, the government made a series of emergency medical interventions and increased spending to revive the economy. In both these efforts, district administration authorities were actively involved.
Which of the following action(s) are plausible?

options.A: In future, the government can make district administration authorities responsible for protecting health of citizens and reviving the economy.
options.B: The government may set up a task force to review the post pandemic situation and ascertain the effectiveness of the measures taken.
options.C: The government may set up a committee to formulate a pandemic management program to minimize losses to life and economy in future.
options.D: The government may take population control measures to minimize pandemic related losses in future.

infoBite: Reviewing what worked and planning for the next pandemic follow from the situation. Making districts solely responsible, or population control, doesn't.

question: Six students, Arif, Balwinder, Chintu, David, Emon and Fulmoni appeared in the GATE-XH exam in 2022. Balwinder scores less than Chintu in XH-B1, but more than Arif in XH-C1. David scores more than Balwinder in XH-C1, and more than Chintu in XH-B1. Emon scores less than David, but more than Fulmoni in XH-B1. Fulmoni scores more than David in XH-C1. Arif scores less than Emon, but more than Fulmoni in XH-B1. Who scores highest in XH-B1?
infoBite: Use only the XH-B1 clues: David > Chintu > Balwinder and David > Emon > Arif > Fulmoni, so David is highest. The XH-C1 clues are distractors.

question:
Select the correct relation between E and F.
E = x/(1+x) and F = −x/(1−x), x > 1
infoBite: For x > 1, E = x/(1+x) is less than 1, while F = −x/(1−x) = x/(x−1) is more than 1. So E < F.

question:
A code language is formulated thus:
Vowels in the original word are replaced by the next vowel from the list of vowels, A-E-I-O-U (For example, E is replaced by I and U is replaced by A). Consonants in the original word are replaced by previous consonant (For example, T is replaced by S and V is replaced by T).
Then how does the word, GOODMORNING appear in the coded language?
infoBite: G→F, O→U, O→U, D→C, M→L, O→U, R→Q, N→M, I→O, N→M, G→F: FUUCLUQMOMF.

question:
The stranger is by nature no "owner of soil" -- soil not only in the physical, but also in the figurative sense of a life-substance, which is fixed, if not in a point in space, at least in an ideal point of the social environment. Although in more intimate relations, he may develop all kinds of charm and significance, as long as he is considered a stranger in the eyes of the other, he is not an "owner of soil." Restriction to intermediary trade, and often (as though sublimated from it) to pure finance, gives him the specific character of mobility. If mobility takes place within a closed group, it embodies that synthesis of nearness and distance which constitutes the formal position of the stranger. For, the fundamentally mobile person comes in contact, at one time or another, with every individual, but is not organically connected, through established ties of kinship, locality, and occupation, with any single one.
What assumptions can be made about the stranger from the passage above?

options.A: The stranger can become an owner of soil through developing all kinds of charm in more intimate relations.
options.B: The stranger cannot become an owner of soil either in the physical or psychological sense.
options.C: The stranger can become an owner of soil through establishing ties of kinship and so on.
options.D: The stranger might become an owner of soil in the physical sense but not in the psychological

infoBite: Adapted from Georg Simmel's essay “The Stranger” (1908): the stranger combines nearness and distance and has no organic ties, so he owns “soil” in neither sense.

question:
L is the only son of A and S. S has one sibling, B, who is married to L’s aunt, K. B is the only son of D. How are L and D related?
Select the possible option(s):
infoBite: B is D's only son, so B's sibling S must be a daughter, i.e. L's mother. D is L's maternal grandparent; D's gender isn't given, so both B and D.

question:
Five segments of a sentence are given below. The first and fifth segments are at their correct positions, while the middle three segments (represented by 2, 3, and 4) are jumbled up. Choose the correct order of the segments so that they form a coherent sentence:
1. Consumed multitudes are jostling and shoving inside me
2. and guided only by the memory of a large white bedsheet with a roughly circular hole some seven inches in diameter cut into the center,
3. clutching at the dream of that holey, mutilated square of linen, which is my talisman, my open-sesame,
4. I must commence the business of remaking my life from the point at which it really began,
5. some thirty-two years before anything as obvious, as present, as my clock-ridden, crime-stained birth.
infoBite: The sentence is from the first chapter of Rushdie's Midnight's Children (1981), “The Perforated Sheet” — the sheet through which Aadam Aziz first examined Naseem.

question:
“I told you the truth,” I say yet again, “Memory’s truth, because memory has its own special kind. It selects, eliminates, alters, exaggerates, minimizes, glorifies, and vilifies also; but in the end it creates its own reality, its heterogeneous but usually coherent versions of events; and no sane human being ever trusts someone else’s version more than his own.”
What are the different ways in which ‘truth’ can be understood from the passage?

options.A: Truth is what can be verified by hard empirical evidence.
options.B: Truth is based on what can be perceived by the senses.
options.C: Truth is the product of memory that is fallible, selective and slanted.
options.D: Truth is contingent on the observer and can only be partial.

infoBite: Saleem Sinai defends “memory's truth” to Padma in Midnight's Children — a key statement of the novel's unreliable narration. Midnight's Children also appears in Q23 and Q62 of this paper.

question: A firm needs both skilled labour and unskilled labour for the production of cloth. The wage of skilled labour is Rs. 40,000 per month, and that of unskilled labour is Rs. 15,000 per month. The total wage bill of the firm for the production of cloth is Rs. 23,75,000 in a month for 100 labour. How many skilled labour are employed by the firm (in Integer)?

Select the odd word and write the option number as answer:
(1) Lek (2) Zloty (3) Diner (4) Drachma (5) Real
infoBite: Lek (Albania), złoty (Poland), drachma (Greece, before the euro) and real (Brazil) are currencies. “Diner” is not — the currency is the dinar.

question: Who published the novel The Bell Jar under the pseudonym Victoria Lucas?
infoBite: The Bell Jar came out in January 1963 as by “Victoria Lucas”, a month before Plath's death; it appeared under her own name in 1966. Pseudonyms were also asked in GATE 2024 (Orwell).

question: In which collection did Walt Whitman’s poem “Song of Myself” first appear?
infoBite: “Song of Myself” opened the first edition of Leaves of Grass (1855) without a title; it got its final title in 1881. The Golden Bough is J. G. Frazer's study of myth and ritual.

question: Who wrote the introduction to Rabindranath Tagore’s Gitanjali?
infoBite: Yeats introduced Gitanjali: Song Offerings (London, 1912). Tagore won the Nobel Prize in 1913, the first non-European laureate.

question:
Identify the title of the poem in which the following lines appear:
“He was found by the Bureau of Statistics to be
One against whom there was no official complaint,
And all the reports on his conduct agree
That, in the modern sense of an old-fashioned word, he was a saint
For in everything he did he served the greater community.”
works: In Memory of W. B. Yeats
infoBite: Auden's satire on the conforming, statistically perfect citizen (1939), collected in Another Time (1940). All four options are Auden poems; Q53 of this paper quotes the Yeats elegy.

question:
Identify the point of view used in the following passage:
“You are not the kind of guy who would be at a place like this at this time of the morning. But here you are, and you cannot say that the terrain is entirely unfamiliar, though the details are fuzzy.”
infoBite: Second-person narration addresses the protagonist as “you”. The passage opens Jay McInerney's Bright Lights, Big City (1984); Calvino's If on a Winter's Night a Traveller (Q64) also uses it.

question: Which of the following is a novel by Charles Dickens?
infoBite: The Old Curiosity Shop (1840–41) follows Little Nell. The Old Wives' Tale (1908) is Arnold Bennett's; The Old Bachelor (1693) is Congreve's first comedy.

question:
Which linguistic process can be seen in the formation of the following words?
i. smog, ii. brunch, iii. motel iv. telecast
infoBite: Blends fuse parts of two words: smoke + fog, breakfast + lunch, motor + hotel, television + broadcast. Backformation removes a supposed affix (edit from editor).

question: Which writer is credited with the ‘chutneyfication’ of Indian English?
infoBite: In Midnight's Children (1981) Saleem, who works in a pickle factory, speaks of the “chutnification of history”; the term is now used for Rushdie's hybrid, Hindi-laced English.

question: Whom would you associate the term ‘simulacra’ with?
infoBite: Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation (1981) describes hyperreality, where copies without originals replace the real.

question: In Plato’s idea of the Republic there is no place for the ___________.
infoBite: In the Republic (Books III and X) Plato banishes poets: poetry imitates an imitation, “thrice removed” from truth, and stirs the passions. Aristotle's Poetics answers him.

question: What was Aristotle’s definition of hubris?

options.B: A false sense of pride which eventually causes the character’s downfall
options.C: An ability to imagine the future

infoBite: Hubris is overweening pride that leads the hero to defy the gods or moral order. Don't confuse it with hamartia (“error of judgement”, option A's “tragic flaw”), the term Aristotle uses in the Poetics.
note: The Poetics itself names hamartia, not hubris; the official key accepts B as the standard definition.

question: Stephen Dedalus is a recurring character in the works of _________.
works: A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man
infoBite: Stephen Dedalus appears in Stephen Hero, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916) and Ulysses (1922). He was asked again in GATE 2024.

question: Which of the following novels opens with the sentence, “It is a truth universally acknowledged that a single man in possession of a good fortune must be in want of a wife.”?
infoBite: The ironic opening of Pride and Prejudice (1813), first drafted as “First Impressions”. All four options are Austen novels.

question: Which of the following novels by Chinua Achebe derives its title from W. B. Yeats’s poem “The Second Coming”?
infoBite: “Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold” is from “The Second Coming” (1920). No Longer at Ease (1960) takes its title from Eliot's “Journey of the Magi”. Things Fall Apart was also asked in GATE 2026.

question: Identify the novels that deal with the trauma of Partition:

options.A: Shauna Singh Baldwin’s What the Body Remembers
options.D: Kamala Markandaya’s Nectar in a Sieve

infoBite: What the Body Remembers (1999) follows two Sikh women up to Partition; The Shadow Lines (1988) ties Partition to the 1964 riots in Dhaka and Calcutta. Cry, the Peacock (1963) is psychological; Nectar in a Sieve (1954) is about rural poverty.

question: Which of the following writers are associated with the Theatre of the Absurd?

options.B: James Joyce’s Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man

infoBite: Spivak's translation of Of Grammatology (1976), with her long Translator's Preface, made Derrida widely known in English.

infoBite: Named for the Lake District, the label began as a sneer in the Edinburgh Review. Southey became Poet Laureate in 1813; Byron mocks him in the dedication of Don Juan.

question: Choose from the following options the type of drama that is intended by the author to be read rather than to be performed:
infoBite: Closet drama is meant to be read: Milton's Samson Agonistes, Byron's Manfred, Shelley's Prometheus Unbound. Kitchen-sink drama is 1950s British realism (Look Back in Anger).

question: Who said, “Poetry makes nothing happen”?
works: In Memory of W. B. Yeats
infoBite: From Part II of Auden's “In Memory of W. B. Yeats” (1939): poetry changes nothing, yet it survives as a way of happening. Auden also appears in Q30.

question:

note: Marked MSQ in the official key with a single correct answer, A.

question: Which of the following works may be described as novels in verse?

question: Which of the following critics belong to the deconstructionist school?
infoBite: De Man and Hillis Miller (with Geoffrey Hartman and Harold Bloom) formed the “Yale School” that brought Derrida's deconstruction to American criticism. Kate Soper is a philosopher of nature and ecology.

question: Cleanth Brooks’s definition of ‘paradox’ in poetry foregrounds the following qualities:

options.D: Omniscience and death of the author

infoBite: In “The Language of Paradox” (The Well Wrought Urn, 1947) Brooks calls paradox the language of poetry, working through wonder and irony; his key example is Donne's “The Canonization”.

question: Two examples of magic realist fiction include:
infoBite: Rushdie's Midnight's Children (1981) and Grass's The Tin Drum (1959), whose Oskar refuses to grow, mix the marvellous with history. The English Teacher (1945) is realist; Tom Jones (1749) is a comic novel. Magic realism was also asked in GATE 2024.

question: Ferdinand de Saussure differentiates language in terms of:
infoBite: Course in General Linguistics (1916, compiled after his death from students' notes): langue is the shared system, parole the individual utterance. Metaphor/metonymy is Roman Jakobson's pair.

options.A: Analyzing the implications of a text for environmental concerns

question:

infoBite: Net outflow per minute is 34 − V/10 − V/6, and it must equal V/60. So 34 = 17V/60, giving V = 120 litres.

question:

question:
A game consists of spinning an arrow around a stationary disk. When the arrow comes to rest, there are eight equally likely outcomes. It could come to rest in any one of the sectors numbered 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 or 8.
Two such disks are used in a game where their arrows are independently spun.
What is the probability that the sum of the numbers on the resulting sectors upon spinning the two disks is equal to 8 after the arrows come to rest?
infoBite: There are 8 × 8 = 64 outcomes. Pairs adding to 8 are (1,7), (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2), (7,1) — 7 of them, so 7/64.
note: The original shows a picture of the numbered disk; the text is enough to solve it.

question:

infoBite: P has 4 children with 3 girls, so 1 boy. R's girls = P's boys = 1, so R has 1 + 4 = 5 boys.

question:
For a painting to succeed, it is essential that the painter and his public agree about what is significant. The subject of the painting may have a personal meaning for the painter or a common person; but there can also be the possibility of their agreement on its general meaning. It is at this point that the culture of the society and the period in question precedes the artists and her/his art. Renaissance art would have meant nothing to the Aztecs, and vice versa. If, to some extent, a few intellectuals can appreciate them both today, it is because their culture is a historical one. Its inspiration is history and all known developments to date.
According to the passage, which of the following is/are NOT necessarily among the attributes needed for a painter to succeed?

options.B: The painter is able to communicate and justify the significance of its subject selection.
options.C: The painter and the public agree on what is significant.
options.D: The painting of the subjects is driven by public demand.

infoBite: The passage says only agreement on significance is essential; personal meaning is merely possible (“may”), and public demand is never required.

question:

Disease is transmitted when sewage and drinking water come into contact. Children are particularly vulnerable. In some of the poorest countries the infant mortality rate is high. The separation of sewage and the supply of clean drinking water are the domain of civil engineers, and their work makes a significant contribution to public health. That contribution was recognized when public sanitation was voted the greatest medical breakthrough, beating the discoveries including antibiotics and vaccines in a poll organized by the British Medical Journal.
Identify the statement(s), which is/are NOT TRUE according to the passage.

options.A: Children are less prone to water borne diseases.
options.B: The infant mortality rate was high in economically weaker countries.
options.C: The provision of sewage and drinking water should be adequately separated from each other.
options.D: The literature states that the public health and sanitation was never given its due importance.

question:
Shark’s teeth have evolved to correspond to the diet of each particular species of shark. Consequently, the teeth of the great white shark bear little resemblance to those of the bull shark or nurse shark. There were essentially four different shark diets and thus four varieties of shark teeth. Sharks that feed on fish have needle like teeth, perfect for spearing and ripping. Sharks that eat mammals such as seals and sea lions have heavy, serrated teeth, typically triangular on the upper jaw and pointed on the lower jaw. Shark that feed in the benthic zone of the ocean have flattened teeth for crushing the shell of the creatures they find scuttling in the sand or clinging to rocks. Sharks that bask have teeth that are largely non-functional; these sharks filter food from the water by passing it through their gills.
Which of the following is/are the CORRECT inference(s) as per the passage?

options.A: Shark’s teeth are not specially designed for slaughter.
options.B: The shape of the shark’s teeth relates to its prey.
options.C: Some species of sharks filter food through their gills.
options.D: Shark’s teeth relate to its diet.

infoBite: Each tooth type matches a diet (needle, serrated, flattened, non-functional), and basking sharks filter food through their gills.

question: Who amongst the following popularised the term ‘objective correlative’, which is often used in formalist criticism?

question: Which of the following critics preferred Shakespeare’s comedies to his tragedies?

question: Who among the following has been credited with laying the foundation of comparative literature by Russian Formalists?

question: Lyrical Ballads, considered to be the manifesto of Romantic Poetry, was first published in the year ________.

question:

question: What does gynocriticism recommend as an approach to literature?

question:

question: Which of the following terms does not form a part of seven types of ambiguities propounded by William Empson?

question: Which of the following poem(s) has/have been influenced by Hindu philosophy?
